sections.html:
Texas has no state property tax. What you owe is the sum of separate levies from the county, your school district, usually a city, and sometimes a hospital, junior college or other special district, all applied to the same house.

Value comes from the local appraisal district, whose chief appraiser looks at every parcel as it stood on January 1 and also processes exemption requests. A review board settles disputes. In many places the county tax assessor-collector sends a single combined statement each October on behalf of all the units.

Here are the ten dates a homeowner should know.

Texas property tax dates for a homeowner
DateWhat happens
Jan. 1Value, exemption status and the year's tax lien are fixed
Apr. 1 or soon afterValue notices go out for single-family homesteads
Apr. 30Deadline for many exemption applications
May 1 or soon afterValue notices for other property
May 15Protest deadline, unless 30 days after the notice is later
July 25Chief appraiser certifies the roll
Sept. 29Most units adopt rates by this date, or within 60 days of the roll if later
Oct. 1Bills mailed
Nov. 30 and June 30Halves of a split payment
Jan. 31Final day without delinquency

Your bill arrives in October. January is the last month to pay without penalty.

Once the certified roll arrives, most units figure two benchmarks before voting. The no-new-revenue rate would raise the same money as last year from the same properties. The voter-approval rate is a ceiling, and a unit that wants to exceed it must go to the voters at the next uniform election date.

Each unit posts both rates on its homepage, announces the vote date in its notice, and, unless it is very small, holds a public hearing. You cannot argue a rate at your own protest hearing, only your value.

Money still owed when January closes goes past due on February 1. Six percent penalty and one percent interest land that very day. From then on the penalty creeps up a point every month until it tops out at twelve percent in July. Interest never stops and has no ceiling.

A unit that has retained a collection lawyer may add up to a fifth on top. Statute gives you 21 days to pay a bill, so a statement mailed after January 10 pushes the due date back. One dated January 15 is not past due until March 1.

Older or disabled owners may pay in four installments. The first falls due by February 1, then March 31, May 31 and July 31. Miss one and you owe six percent of it plus a monthly one percent.

  • You can ask in writing, before day 181, for the penalty and interest to be forgiven, provided you paid within 21 days of finding out you were behind.
  • Plans stretching up to 36 months exist at some offices, and a residence homestead is entitled to one.
  • Owners past 65 or disabled may split even a current bill four ways.

Your homestead exemption is the largest discount available. A school district must knock $140,000 off the taxable value. Any other unit can choose a percentage cut instead, up to 20 percent, with a floor of $5,000.

  • Being 65 or older, or qualifying as disabled, adds $60,000 more off the school bill.
  • A service-connected disability rating takes between $5,000 and $12,000 off, and a house owned by someone rated 100 percent pays nothing.
  • A widow or widower aged 55 or more may inherit the late spouse's over-65 benefit in some cases.

File by the end of April. Bought after January 1 from an owner who never applied? You can still apply for that year.

sections.h2: What happens if taxes are never paid
sections.html:
Expect delinquent notices first, then perhaps a payment plan, then a lawsuit with court costs piled onto the balance. The suit can end with an auction conducted by a constable or a contracted agent. Sales are announced locally, so watch the county clerk and tax office websites.

Rights after the sale depend on what kind of property it was. Homestead, agricultural and mineral land can be redeemed within two years, and the former owner also has two years to claim excess sale proceeds. If you inherit a house with unpaid years on it, call the tax office quickly, because a payment plan may still be available.

sections.h2: Timing a sale around the tax year
sections.html:
January 1 fixes the lien, October 1 brings the bill and February 1 starts penalties. So a house that changes hands in spring is billed months later, and the closing agent splits the year between the two parties on the settlement statement. Listing in winter lets you clear the prior year before it turns past due.

Spring is also when appraisal notices land. If one arrives while you are under contract, tell your agent. A lower value after a protest changes the amount being split.

sections.h2: Limits on how fast a homestead bill can grow
sections.html:
Two guardrails protect homeowners. Once the exemption has been active a year, appraised value cannot jump more than 10 percent annually, new improvements aside.

Owners past 65 or disabled also receive a school tax ceiling locked in at the qualifying year, and a share of it can travel with them to another Texas residence. Counties, cities and junior college districts can adopt ceilings too, so ask each whether it did.

sections.h2: If the appraisal looks too high
sections.html:
Your first stop is the appraisal review board. The cutoff is May 15 or a month after the notice, whichever lands later. Unhappy with the outcome? Choose district court, regular binding arbitration, or, once the board's value tops $1,000,000, the State Office of Administrative Hearings.

Whichever path you pick, pay at least the part you do not dispute before the due date. Our protest guide covers the hearing step by step.

sections.h2: What to bring to the tax office
sections.html:
Carry the account number, the address and the name on the deed. Ask for this year's amount, every earlier unpaid year, accrued penalty and interest, and any plan or waiver attached to the account. Request it in writing so everyone at closing works from the same numbers.

Inheriting? Find out which exemptions are active. An heir living there may need to refile personally.

sections.h2: Selling a house with taxes owed
sections.html:
The lien rides with the property, so no insurer will cover a buyer until earlier years are settled. Whoever owned on January 1 answers for that year even after selling and can be sued for it.

At closing the escrow officer pays old amounts out of your sale money and divides the current year. Get a tax certificate from the assessor-collector listing every unit, then check it against the settlement statement.

  • Look for past-due years, penalties and attorney fees.
  • Ask whether a payment plan is running.
  • The new owner applies for the homestead exemption afterward.

If back taxes, repairs and showings sound exhausting, a cash sale is another option. The balance gets paid from the proceeds at closing either way.

faqs.q: Does Texas collect a state property tax?
faqs.a: No, the state collects none. Counties, cities, schools and special districts set their own rates and keep the money.

faqs.q: When is Texas property tax due?
faqs.a: Statements mail in October and are payable on receipt. Whatever remains after January 31 is past due on February 1. A split-payment arrangement, where offered, uses November 30 and June 30.

faqs.q: How much is the late charge?
faqs.a: Day one brings a six percent penalty and one percent interest. The penalty rises a point each month, reaching twelve percent in July.

faqs.q: How big is the homestead exemption?
faqs.a: A school district exempts $140,000, and owners who are older or disabled get $60,000 more. Other units may offer their own exemptions.

faqs.q: Can back taxes come out of a sale?
faqs.a: Yes. The closing agent typically pays them from the sale money, since the lien stays attached to the house.
